segments.text: Population geography studies where people live, how populations change and what those patterns mean for resources and development. Settlement and urban geography study how villages and cities are arranged internally and across regions.
This is a model-and-map topic. Learn demographic processes first, then world distribution, then city structure and urban problems.

items.text: Population growth
: Population changes through births, deaths and migration. Natural increase is births minus deaths, while total population change also includes net migration.
Population structure
: Age and sex composition can be shown through population pyramids. Structure influences schooling, labour force, healthcare, pensions and dependency patterns.
Demographic transition

: The demographic transition model describes a broad historical shift from high birth/death rates toward low birth/death rates as societies undergo economic and social change. Real countries do not always follow the model perfectly.
World population distribution

: Population is uneven because of climate, water, soils, relief, jobs, accessibility, history and political conditions. Dense regions often combine productive environments with long settlement histories and economic opportunities.
Over- and under-population

: Overpopulation is best understood relative to resources, technology, consumption and carrying capacity rather than as a fixed number. Under-population refers to situations where population may be too small to use resources or support services efficiently.
Models of internal city structure

: The concentric-zone model describes rings, the sector model emphasizes wedges along transport routes, and the multiple-nuclei model sees several activity centers. These are simplified models, not exact maps of every city.
World urban patterns
: Urbanization differs by region in timing, speed, city size and network structure. Megacities, metropolitan regions and smaller cities may face different opportunities and pressures.
Settlement theories

: Settlement geography examines site, situation, spacing, hierarchy and service areas. Central-place ideas explain how settlements of different sizes may provide different ranges of goods and services.
Urban problems

: Common issues include housing shortages, informal settlements, congestion, pollution, unequal services, waste, heat, flooding and social segregation. Causes usually involve rapid growth plus planning, land and governance constraints.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

Population changes through births, deaths and migration. At the national level, natural increase equals births minus deaths; total population change adds net migration. These components affect not only total numbers but also age structure, labour force, service demand and settlement patterns.

items.text: Fertility

: Fertility is influenced by age at marriage, education, child survival, contraception, labour-force participation, social norms and economic expectations. It should not be treated as a purely biological constant.
Mortality

: Mortality patterns reflect health care, nutrition, sanitation, disease, income, conflict and age structure. Improvements in child survival often precede fertility decline during demographic transition.
Migration

: Migration redistributes population and is shaped by opportunities, costs, social networks, conflict, environmental stress and policy. Push-pull language is useful but should not hide the fact that decisions are constrained by resources and institutions.
Stage 1
: High birth and death rates produce slow growth in the classical model. Few contemporary states fit this historical stage exactly.
Stage 2
: Death rates fall with improvements in food, sanitation and health while birth rates remain high, producing rapid natural increase.
Stage 3
: Birth rates decline as urbanization, education, changing family economics and access to contraception alter reproductive behaviour.
Stage 4
: Both birth and death rates are low, producing slow growth or stability.
Possible Stage 5
: Some models add a stage of very low fertility and population ageing or decline. The extension is descriptive and countries do not follow identical paths.
Population pyramid

: A broad base indicates a large share of children; a more rectangular shape reflects lower fertility and longer survival; a narrow base with larger older cohorts can indicate ageing. Pyramids summarize structure, not just total population.

blocks.text: Population distribution and the idea of overpopulation

items.text: Physical factors
: Water, fertile soils, moderate climate and accessible lowlands encourage dense settlement, while extreme cold, aridity, high mountains and disease environments can limit it.
Economic and historical factors
: Industrialization, ports, transport corridors, long settlement history and political stability can support dense populations even where natural conditions are not ideal.
Overpopulation

: Overpopulation is a relationship among population, consumption, technology, institutions and carrying capacity. Density alone is not enough: a dense region can sustain high living standards with productive infrastructure, while a sparse region can face severe resource stress.
Underpopulation
: A small population may limit market size, labour supply or service efficiency in resource-rich or very large territories, but the concept is context-dependent.
Site
: The physical characteristics of the location itself, such as water supply, relief or defensibility.
Situation
: The location relative to routes, markets, resources and other settlements.
Hierarchy
: Settlements vary in size and in the range and order of services they provide. Higher-order centres support specialized functions that require larger market thresholds.
Central place theory

: Christaller's model explains how settlements could form a regular hierarchy if consumers use nearest centres and space is uniform. It clarifies threshold and range but real transport networks, politics and uneven population disturb the ideal hexagonal pattern.

blocks.text: Urban growth and internal city models

items.text: Urbanization

: Urbanization is an increasing share of population living in urban areas; urban growth is an increase in the absolute urban population. A city can grow even when the national urbanization percentage changes slowly.
Burgess concentric zones

: Burgess described city growth in rings around a central business district, reflecting early twentieth-century Chicago. It is historically important but weak for polycentric and automobile-oriented cities.
Hoyt sector model
: Hoyt emphasized wedge-shaped sectors extending along transport routes, especially for higher-income housing and industry.
Multiple-nuclei model
: Harris and Ullman argued that cities develop several activity centres because different functions have distinct accessibility and land requirements.
Contemporary form

: Modern metropolitan regions can include edge cities, gated developments, informal settlements, industrial corridors and multiple employment centres, so classic models are starting points rather than exact maps.

blocks.text: Urban problems as spatial and governance problems

items.text: Housing

: Rapid demand, land-market constraints and weak planning can produce overcrowding, high prices and informal settlements. Informality is not simply a personal choice; it can reflect exclusion from formal land and credit systems.
Transport
: Congestion arises when trip demand exceeds network capacity and when land use creates long journeys. Public transport, walkability and demand management can complement road expansion.
Environment
: Air pollution, waste, heat islands, flood risk and water stress often concentrate unevenly across neighbourhoods.
Segregation
: Income, ethnicity, land values, discrimination and planning can create spatial separation. Segregation shapes access to schools, jobs, health care and exposure to environmental risk.
Governance
: Urban problems are rarely solved by one engineering project. Land administration, finance, service coordination and metropolitan governance are central.

segments.text: Pakistan's 2023 Population and Housing Census recorded 241,499,431 people. The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics reported 93,884,702 people in urban areas and 147,614,729 in rural areas. These figures are useful for demonstrating the scale of settlement change, but urban definitions and administrative boundaries should always be checked when comparing across years.

The same census shows that Pakistan's demographic questions are not only about total population. Age structure, fertility, migration, city growth and service capacity determine how population pressure is experienced in different regions.
Reading the flow: each step creates the conditions for the next; the arrows show sequence or influence, not inevitability unless the text explicitly says so.

Use maps to explain population distribution rather than memorizing country rankings.
For urban problems use cause → spatial pattern → social/environmental effect → planning response.

rows: Avoid this error Do not call every dense country “overpopulated.” Overpopulation is a relationship among population, resources, technology, consumption and capacity.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Explain demographic components and transition, world distribution and population structure, then settlement hierarchy, urban models, world urbanization and city problems.
• Federal Public Service Commission, Revised Scheme and Syllabus for CSS Competitive Examination (CE-2016 and onwards).
• United Nations DESA, World Population Prospects 2024; Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, National Census Report 2023.
• Population changes through fertility, mortality and migration.
• Population structure matters as much as total size.
• Urban models simplify reality but help compare city form.
• Urban problems are spatial and institutional, not simply the result of “too many people.”
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
